items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 692): A hospital worker wears a film badge, a technician uses a Geiger-Muller tube, and a researcher uses a sodium iodide crystal that flashes when struck. Identify the detection method used by each, and name the three general means of detecting subatomic particles.

answer.html: (1) The film badge uses exposure of photographic film. (2) The Geiger-Muller tube uses ionization of matter (a gas); cloud and bubble chambers also work this way. (3) The crystal causes matter to emit photons (scintillation). These are the three general means.

check.html: Each device matches one of the three categories shown for detectors in the lesson.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 19: In a cloud chamber the magnetic field points into the page. Two particles move upward on the page from the same point; particle A curves to the left and particle B curves to the right. Which is positive and which is negative? Explain why they bend in different directions.

body.html: → 𝐵 into the page; both velocities up the page; A curves left, B curves right.
A charged particle in a magnetic field feels a force perpendicular to its velocity, 𝐹= 𝑞𝑣𝐵, with direction given by the right-hand rule for a positive charge and reversed for a negative charge.
For a positive charge moving up the page with → 𝐵 into the page, the right-hand rule (→𝑣× → 𝐵) gives a force to the left. A negative charge feels the opposite force, to the right.

answer.html: Particle A (curving left) is positive and particle B (curving right) is negative. The tracks bend in opposite directions because the magnetic force on a moving charge reverses when the sign of the charge reverses.

check.html: An electron-positron pair made at one point in a magnetic field curves in just this way.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 693): How does the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider differ from a Geiger-Muller tube?

answer.html: A Geiger-Muller tube only clicks when ionizing radiation passes through it, so it counts particles but reveals little else. CMS is a huge array of many layers of electronic detectors (tracking, energy-measuring, and muon detectors in a strong magnetic field) that records the positions, momenta, and energies of the particles from each collision, analyzed by computer, with rapid selection of the interesting events.

check.html: One device counts; the other reconstructs complete events.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 694): The name "meson" comes from a Greek word meaning "middle." Why was it an appropriate name? Use the mass energies electron 0.511 MeV, pion

body.html: Compare the pion's mass energy with the other two.
Mass and energy are equivalent, so masses can be compared as mass energies.

answer.html: The first mesons found had masses between the electron and the proton: the pion is about 273 times heavier than an electron but only about 1 / 6.7 as heavy as a proton. "Middle" described that mass.

check.html: The pion lies between the two in mass energy.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 694): Classify each as a quark, a lepton, or a hadron: muon, strange quark, kaon, tau neutrino, neutron, up quark, positron. Distinguish between quarks and leptons.

answer.html: Quarks: strange quark, up quark. Leptons: muon, tau neutrino, positron. Hadrons (made of quarks): kaon (a meson) and neutron (a baryon). Quarks feel the strong force and combine to make hadrons; leptons do not feel the strong force and do not form hadrons. Both are elementary particles that come in six flavors.

check.html: A kaon and a neutron are made of quarks, so they are hadrons and not elementary.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problems (Pair production) 36: Pair production creates a particle and its antiparticle. Name the particle that is created along with each: (a) an electron, (b) an antineutron, (c) an antimuon, (d) a proton.

body.html: Pair production creates a particle together with its antiparticle (same mass, opposite charge).
(a) the antiparticle of the electron is the positron; (b) of the antineutron, the neutron; (c) of the antimuon, the muon; (d) of the proton, the antiproton.

answer.html: (a) positron; (b) neutron; (c) muon; (d) antiproton.

check.html: Each pair has equal masses and opposite charge (or zero).

body.html: A pair requires two muon masses: 2(1.06 × 10<sup>8</sup> eV) = 2.12 × 10<sup>8</sup> eV.

check.html: About 207 times the electron pair threshold of 1.02 MeV (1.02 × 207 ≈211 MeV).

body.html: Energy conservation: for a pair at rest the total gamma energy is 2𝑚<sub>e</sub>𝑐<sup>2</sup> = 1.02 MeV = 1022 keV.

answer.html: 3.17 × 10<sup>2</sup> keV (using 1.02 MeV gives 315 keV, the same to 2 significant figures: 3.2 × 10<sup>2</sup> keV).

check.html: Positive and smaller than the total.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 3) 41: Research one experimental result that showed the original Standard Model was incomplete (for example, neutrino oscillations) and summarize it.

body.html: This is a research prompt. A sample summary follows.

Experiments that detected neutrinos from the Sun and from cosmic-ray collisions in the atmosphere found fewer of one type than predicted, and later experiments showed that neutrinos change from one type to another as they travel. That is only possible if neutrinos have mass, but the original Standard Model treated them as massless. Other limitations: the model does not include gravity, dark matter, or dark energy, and does not explain the matter- antimatter imbalance.

answer.html: Neutrino oscillation experiments showed that neutrinos have mass, so the original Standard Model had to be extended; the model also still leaves out gravity, dark matter and dark energy, and the matter-antimatter asymmetry.

check.html: Each limitation is consistent with the "Testing the Standard Model" section.

items.title: of an alpha particle (+2𝑒) at a distance of 1.5 × 10−14 m from the center of the gold nucleus. Use

question.html: 𝑘= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> N · m<sup>2</sup> / C<sup>2</sup> and 𝑒= 1.60 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> C.

body.html: An alpha particle is positively charged and is repelled by the positive nucleus (a Coulomb barrier), with potential energy 𝑈= 𝑘𝑞<sub>1</sub>𝑞<sub>2</sub> / 𝑟. A neutron has no charge and feels no electric repulsion.

answer.html: The alpha particle needs roughly 15 MeV of kinetic energy to get that close to the gold nucleus, so it must be accelerated in a machine. A neutron feels no electric repulsion, so it can approach even at low energy until the strong force captures it.

check.html: This is why neutrons are effective at inducing reactions in heavy nuclei.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 3) 43: Protons circulate clockwise as viewed from above in a circular accelerator ring. In which direction must the magnetic field of the bending magnets point?

body.html: Charge +𝑒; the force must point toward the center of the ring (centripetal).
Magnetic force →
𝐵 (right-hand rule).

Take east as +𝑥, north as +𝑦, up as +𝑧. Clockwise from above, a proton at the east side of the ring moves south (−𝑦). The force must point west (−𝑥, toward the center). Try → 𝐵 up: south × up = ( −𝑦) × ( + 𝑧) = −𝑥, which is west. So → 𝐵 points upward.

answer.html: The bending magnets' field points vertically upward.

check.html: Reversing → 𝐵 would push the protons outward and out of the ring.

items.title: Engineering and Technology Problem Engineering and Technology, 3D Thinking: Engage in Argument from Evidence: Write an argument about whether nuclear fission power should be expanded over the next few decades.

body.html: An argument states a claim, gives evidence, and gives reasoning.

Evidence for: one kilogram of uranium-235 releases about 7.5 × 10<sup>13</sup> J, roughly 3 × 10<sup>6</sup> times the energy of a kilogram of coal; a fission plant produces no carbon dioxide while operating. Evidence against: the fission products and spent fuel stay radioactive for a long time and must be stored safely; accidents, though rare, are serious; reactors are expensive to build.

answer.html: Fission power should be expanded cautiously because of its enormous energy per kilogram of fuel and lack of operating carbon emissions, provided waste storage and safety systems are improved; the remaining problems are engineering and policy challenges that evidence and research can address.

check.html: Each point can be supported by data on energy per reaction, fuel quantity, and waste half-lives.

items.title: Data Analysis Lab, Claims 1–3: Can you evaluate claims from a Web site? (Questions 1–3). Claims: (1) A company says it built a reactor that gets energy by fusing lead nuclei. (2) A museum says carbon dating shows a wooden artifact is 80,000 years old. (3) A lab says it used a cyclotron to accelerate alpha particles to high speed.

body.html: For each claim decide whether it is likely true (question 1), what evidence supports that (question 2), and give the reasoning (question 3).
Fusion releases energy only for nuclei lighter than iron-56; carbon-14 has a 5730-year half-life; accelerators use electric and magnetic fields, which act on charged particles.

For claim 2: the number of half-lives is 80, 000 / 5730 = 13.96, and (1 / 2)<sup>13.96</sup> = 6.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup>, so only about 0.006% of the carbon-14 would remain, too little to measure reliably. Claim Likely true? Evidence Reasoning 1. Fusing lead for energy Not as stated Binding energy per nucleon is most negative near Fe-56 and less negative for lead Fusing nuclei heavier than iron produces less tightly bound nuclei, so it would take energy rather than release it 2. Wood 80,000 years old by carbon dating Not reliable C-14 half-life is 5730 years After about 14 half-lives only 6.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> of the carbon-14 is left, too little to date accurately 3. Cyclotron accelerates alpha particles Likely true Alpha particles are charged (+2𝑒) Electric and magnetic fields can accelerate and steer charged particles

answer.html: (1) Not likely true as stated (energy-releasing fusion stops at iron). (2) Not reliable: too old for carbon dating. (3) Likely true: alpha particles are charged and can be accelerated.

check.html: Each decision follows from a principle stated in the module.

items.title: Module Wrap-Up Problem Revisit the Phenomenon: How does a fission power plant produce energy and how is it controlled? (CER)

body.html: Fission of heavy nuclei releases the energy of the mass lost; moderators and control rods regulate the chain reaction. Work (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning): Claim: A fission plant gets its energy from splitting uranium-235 nuclei; the chain reaction is controlled by slowing neutrons and absorbing extra neutrons. Evidence: One fission releases about 184 MeV because the products have 0.198 u less mass; each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons; binding energy per nucleon is less negative for 𝐴= 235 than for 𝐴≈100 to 140. Reasoning: The fission fragments are more tightly bound than uranium, so mass becomes energy (𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>). Water as a moderator slows neutrons (light nuclei remove the most energy per collision), and control rods absorb neutrons so that on average only one neutron per fission causes another fission.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: fission energy is the mass lost in splitting the nucleus, and the chain reaction is controlled by regulating the neutrons.

check.html: Consistent with the earlier claim; no revision needed.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 692): Identify three means of detecting subatomic particles

answer.html: (1) Exposure of photographic film. (2) Ionization of matter (such as in Geiger-Müller tubes, cloud and bubble chambers). (3) Causing matter to emit photons (scintillation).

check.html: These are the three labeled in Figure 18.

items.title: Lesson 3, Figure 19: Explain why the trails bend in different directions

body.html: A false-color bubble-chamber photograph (looked at) shows some tracks curving one way and others the opposite way.
A charged particle in a magnetic field feels a force perpendicular to its velocity, 𝐹= 𝑞𝑣𝐵, with direction depending on the sign of the charge.
In the same magnetic field, positive and negative particles moving the same way are pushed in opposite directions, so their tracks curve in opposite directions.

answer.html: The tracks bend in different directions because the particles have opposite electric charges, and the magnetic force on a moving charge reverses direction when the sign of the charge reverses.

check.html: In Figure 24 (pair production) the electron and positron curve in opposite directions.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 693): How does ATLAS differ from the Wilson cloud chamber?

answer.html: A cloud chamber only makes visible trails of charged particles for a person to look at, while ATLAS is a huge array of many electronic detectors (tracking and energy-measuring layers) that records positions, momenta, and energies by computer, handles a billion collisions per second, and selects the interesting events.

check.html: ATLAS is 25 m tall; a cloud chamber is table-top.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 694): Why is "neutrino" an appropriate name?

answer.html: Neutrino means "little neutral one" in Italian. The particle is electrically neutral and has a tiny (nearly zero) mass.

check.html: The name matches Fermi's description.

items.title: Lesson 3, "Get It?" (page 694): Distinguish between quarks and leptons

answer.html: Both are elementary particles with mass and charge, in six flavors each. Quarks feel the strong force and combine to make hadrons (protons, neutrons, mesons); leptons (electrons, muons, neutrinos) do not feel the strong force and do not form hadrons.

check.html: Matches Figure 22.

items.title: Lesson 3, Practice Problems (Pair production) 36: Pair-production partners

body.html: Pair production creates a particle together with its antiparticle (same mass, opposite charge).
(a) antiparticle of the positron is the electron; (b) of the neutron, the antineutron; (c) of the antiproton, the proton; (d) of the muon, the antimuon.

answer.html: (a) electron; (b) antineutron; (c) proton; (d) antimuon (positive muon).

check.html: Each pair has equal masses and opposite charge (or zero).

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 3) 41: Limitations of the Standard Model (research)

body.html: This is a research prompt. Summary of well-known limitations:

The Standard Model does not include gravity; does not explain dark matter or dark energy (together most of the universe); originally treated neutrinos as massless though they have mass; does not explain why matter dominates over antimatter; has many unexplained constants (particle masses, three generations); and does not unify the strong force with the electroweak force. Proposed extensions include supersymmetry, grand unified theories, string theory, and loop quantum gravity.

answer.html: The Standard Model leaves out gravity, dark matter and dark energy, neutrino mass, and the matter-antimatter asymmetry; alternatives such as supersymmetry, grand unified theories, and string theory try to address these but have no confirmed experimental support yet.

check.html: Each limitation is consistent with the "Testing the Standard Model" section.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 3) 42: Proton versus neutron as a projectile

body.html: A proton has charge +𝑒 and is repelled by the positive charge of the nucleus (Coulomb barrier). A neutron has no charge and feels no electric repulsion.
The proton must be accelerated to enough kinetic energy to overcome the repulsion; the neutron can approach even at low energy until the strong force captures it.

answer.html: A proton is positively charged and is repelled by the positively charged nucleus, so it needs extra energy to get close enough for the strong force to act; a neutral neutron feels no such repulsion.

check.html: This is why neutrons are effective at inducing fission.

question.html: Why does the bottom set of tracks curve less than the top pair?

body.html: Looking at the figure: the top pair spirals tightly; the bottom pair is nearly straight (a slight curve).
In a magnetic field, the radius is 𝑟=<sub> </sub><sup>𝑚𝑣</sup> <sub>𝑞</sub><sub>𝐵</sub> (or 𝑝/ 𝑞𝐵): a larger momentum gives a larger radius, hence less curvature.
Electron and positron have the same mass and charge magnitude in the same field, so a larger radius means larger speed (momentum), i.e. more kinetic energy.

answer.html: The bottom pair has more momentum (they were made by a higher-energy gamma ray and carry more kinetic energy), so their path has a larger radius and curves less. The top pair has little energy and spirals tightly as they lose it.

items.title: Engineering and Technology, 3D Thinking: Engage in Argument from Evidence

question.html: Write an argument about the importance of fusion as a future energy source.

body.html: An argument states a claim, gives evidence, and gives reasoning.

Evidence: fusion of hydrogen releases about 25 MeV per helium nucleus, about a million times more per reaction than a chemical reaction; its fuel (hydrogen) is plentiful; it makes no polluting by-products and is safer than fission. Counter-evidence: it needs temperatures over 150 million degrees C and plasma containment, and currently takes more energy than it gives.

answer.html: Fusion research is worth continuing because the energy released per reaction is enormous, the fuel is abundant, and the waste is limited; the remaining problems (heating, confining, and sustaining the plasma, and cost) are engineering challenges that research can solve.

check.html: Every point is supported by the Engineering and Technology reading.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon: How does the Sun produce energy and how can we replicate it? (CER)

body.html: Fusion powers the Sun; replicating it requires making and confining a hot plasma. Work (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning): Claim: The Sun produces energy by fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium; we can replicate it by heating hydrogen fuel to extremely high temperatures and confining it. Evidence: Four protons fuse to form helium-4 and release about 25 MeV; mass of the products is less than the reactants; the reaction requires about 2 × 10<sup>7</sup> K; binding energy per nucleon increases from hydrogen to iron. Reasoning: The helium nucleus is more tightly bound than four separate protons, so mass is converted to energy ( 𝐸= 𝑚𝑐<sup>2</sup>). High temperature is needed to overcome the repulsion between positive nuclei. On Earth, electromagnets can confine the plasma.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: the Sun's energy is fusion energy, and replication requires heating and confining plasma.

check.html: Consistent with the earlier claim; no revision needed.

body.html: For each claim decide whether it is likely true (question 1), what evidence supports that (question 2), and give the reasoning (question 3).
Iron-56 has the most tightly bound nucleus, so fission of iron releases no energy; carbon-14 has a 5730-year half-life; linear accelerators use electric fields, which act only on charged particles.

For claim 2: (1 / 2)<sup>2000 / 5730</sup> = 0.785, so about 79% of the C-14 would remain after 2000 years, which is easily measurable. Claim Likely true? Evidence Reasoning 1.
